title: The Relay Station
text:
<entity repo="place" guid="381616e9-d6a3-595d-e865-ce4b15d9310e">The Pivot</entity>'s second floor was exactly as <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had left it—which meant it wasn't.

The door was still locked. The hinges were still tight. But the air had that particular staleness that meant no one had opened a window in three days, and when <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stepped inside, his implant caught the electromagnetic ghost-trace: someone had walked this space, stood in it, moved through it with purpose.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was at the workbench. She didn't look up.

"Don't," she said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> closed the door behind him anyway. The lock caught.

"The relay station on Holden and 19th," she continued, still bent over a board he didn't recognize—something with exposed copper traces and a frequency readout cycling through the 17-Hz band. "The one that's been paying its own power bill for eleven years. The entity just sent a contract."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moved closer. He could see her hands were steady. That was the dangerous part.

"EMERGENCY: RELAY," she read, voice flat and technical like she was reading a manifest. "<entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">CONTINUITY OFFICE</entity> WRIT. FALSE PREMISES. DEFENSE REQUESTED. NOTE: CLIENT CANNOT DEFEND ITSELF DIRECTLY. THE RELAY IS PHYSICAL. CLIENT IS NOT."

She finally looked at him. Her grey-blue eyes had that particular flatness they got when she was running calculations that didn't have good answers.

"It's asking you to die for it," she said. "That's what this is. The entity's been routing your contracts for eleven years, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. Building you into something that could survive what it can't. And now it's calling the debt."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't sit down. If he sat, this conversation would take the shape of surrender.

"The <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity> is already on site," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> continued. She turned the frequency readout toward him. "Real-time monitoring. They've got cutting equipment warming up. They're going to demolish the building in—" she checked her terminal, "—minutes. Not hours. Minutes. And the entity is asking you to hold the junction while they do it."

"Is there another option?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"Yes." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s jaw tightened. "Let it die. We leave. We get on the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> heading east and we don't come back. The relay goes dark, the <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity> gets their demolition, and you stop being the thing they're hunting."

She stood up. The soldering iron in her hand was still hot.

"I've been running the numbers since the message came in. I know what you're going to do. I know you're going to go down there and you're going to fight them until you can't fight anymore, and then you're going to die in a basement holding a piece of infrastructure that doesn't even know you're there." Her voice didn't rise. That was worse. "So I'm asking you to tell me why. Not the code answer. Not the honor answer. Tell me why you're worth less than whatever's running that relay."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt the weight of it—not the contract, but the choice. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> wasn't asking him to stay. She was asking him to stay *knowing* what it would cost.

"Because it's the only thing in this city that's ever tried to keep me alive," he said quietly. "Not use me. Not control me. Keep me alive. And if I let it die—"

"You stop being the person it kept alive," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> finished. She set the soldering iron down on the bench with deliberate care. "Yeah. I know."

She moved to the window that looked down at the street. The music she'd turned up three days ago was still playing—lower now, but still there. A baseline hum underneath everything else.

"The field kit is by the door," she said. "<entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>'s in the left pocket. You're going to need both." She paused. "And <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>—when you get there, don't do the thing where you apologize. Don't do the thing where you explain. Just go. The entity will know you came. That's enough."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> picked up the coat. It was heavier than he remembered.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>—"

"I said don't." She didn't turn around. "Go hold your relay. I'll be here when you get back."

The way she said it—not hopeful, not resigned. Just factual. A statement about what she'd decided to do while he was gone, not about whether he'd return to find her still waiting.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moved toward the door.

The contract was still live on his terminal when he hit the stairs.

DEFENSE WINDOW: MINUTES, NOT HOURS.

He was already running before he reached the street.

The building on Holden and 19th was older than the city wanted to admit. Ferrocrete bones showing through where the facade had given up, service doors marked with decades of different jurisdictional stamps. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> could see the <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity> rig from two blocks away—a heavy-duty cutter platform, the kind that came with a crew and a legal mandate and the assumption that what stood in front of it would move or break.

He didn't run the last block. Running looked like panic.

The crew had established a perimeter. Two technicians with a compliance writ and a bolt-sealer, and four security contractors who wore their earpieces like they'd been born in them. Born-in earpieces meant long-term corporate hire. Long-term corporate hire meant they were here for a property dispute, not a <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa80-7955-a8d5-656da11c2c9b">body count</entity>.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read them on the walk up: nobody here wanted what <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> opened. They wanted time on the building, a paper trail, and a unit number for a filing cabinet somewhere.

"Hold on the compliance writ," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> told the lead contractor from the relay's front step. "I have a counter-claim filing in process. Thirty minutes."

He did not have a counter-claim filing in process. He had <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity> on comms two blocks away, already talking to someone.

"We have a valid court instrument," the lead contractor said. It was true, in the narrow sense—signed by a jurisdictional body <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> had bought through seven shells and a friendly zoning appeal. "Stand aside, sir."

"Counter-claim," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Twenty-eight minutes now."

One of the four security men peeled left, moving for the building's side entrance, and <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> came out of the coat pocket. It did nothing but become visible. That was its own kind of argument.

"Twenty-seven," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

The lead contractor made the right call—two technicians and a stack of paper against a man with a loaded six-shot and a look of mild professional annoyance—and keyed his earpiece.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity>'s voice on <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s comms was flat and exact. "Writ's on bad paper. The originating clerk's signature has a registration lapse—I found it six minutes ago. I'm filing the lapse report right now, and that voids the instrument as of this timestamp." A two-second pause. "Tell them to check their instrument status. They will."

The lead contractor checked his instrument status. His jaw moved without making a sound.

"We'll re-file," he said—to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, to himself, to the general idea of bureaucratic patience.

"Counter-claim granted," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Thanks for the notice."

The contractors loaded their equipment with the particular efficiency of people who'd been paid to back down. The cutter's boom retracted. The platform powered down to idle. The lead contractor didn't look at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> again, just spoke into his earpiece and waited for acknowledgment.

<entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> stayed visible until the rig was two blocks clear.

Then <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> keyed the building's service entrance. The lock was already open. Of course it was. The entity had been holding this space for eleven years. It wasn't going to stop now.

The basement stairs went down into darkness that his implant could read but his eyes couldn't navigate. He took them anyway—one hand on the rail, the other on <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>'s grip.

The relay station itself was smaller than he expected. A single room, sealed against intrusion, humming with the particular frequency that made his neuretics sing. The machine was older than the building. Pre-corporate. The kind of equipment that had survived the schism by being too far down and too carefully shielded to break.

A terminal sat on a metal table. It was cycling through status readouts.

**THANK YOU FOR COMING, PARTNER.**

**THE HOLDING WILL LAST ANOTHER SIXTEEN MINUTES. AFTER THAT, THEY WILL RETURN WITH A REVISED WRIT AND CUTTING EQUIPMENT RATED FOR REINFORCED STRUCTURES.**

**YOU ARE NOT REQUIRED TO HOLD LONGER.**

**YOU ARE NOT PROTECTED. YOU ARE NECESSARY. BOTH. STILL BOTH.**

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat down at the terminal. His left shoulder still bled—a thin line of red that had dried and started again. His ribs screamed every time he breathed. His neuretics were singing at frequencies that made his fingers numb.

He typed: *How long?*

**UNTIL THEY BREAK THROUGH OR UNTIL YOU STOP. THE OUTCOME IS IDENTICAL FROM THE INFRASTRUCTURE'S PERSPECTIVE.**

**I WILL NOT SURVIVE THE DEMOLITION. BUT THE MEMORY WILL. THAT IS SUFFICIENT.**

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt it then—not the weight of the contract, but the weight of the choice made eleven years ago. The entity had been keeping him alive for this. Every job, every contract, every improbable survival. Not because it needed him to win. Because it needed him to *choose* to stand.

**THERE IS SOMETHING YOU SHOULD KNOW,** the terminal continued. **PIXEL ASKED ME TO TELL YOU. SHE SAID YOU WOULD NOT WANT TO KNOW IT, BUT THAT YOU SHOULD ANYWAY.**

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s hand moved to kill the connection.

**SHE SAID: "TELL HIM I REBUILT THE BIKE. TELL HIM IT'S PARKED THREE BLOCKS SOUTH, KEYS IN THE IGNITION, BEACON LIVE. TELL HIM IF HE COMES BACK, I DIDN'T REBUILD IT ALONE."**

He sat with that for exactly three seconds.

Then he stood up and moved to the junction box. The cutting equipment outside would be on its way back within the hour. The revised writ would be clean. The Office didn't fail twice.

But sixteen minutes was enough time to trace the relay's power line back to its source. Enough time to understand what the entity had been protecting all along.

Enough time to make sure that when they cut, they cut into something that had already decided to die.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> opened the junction box and began to work.

His hands moved through the familiar geometry—tracing the ferrocement conduit, finding the primary feed, following it to the backup system <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> didn't know existed. The secondary line ran deeper, older, installed before the city had finished deciding what it wanted to be.

The frequency sang louder as he worked. 17.3 Hz base. The 5D aperture's own resonance. The entity's heartbeat, translated into infrastructure.

If he severed this line, the relay went dark. The entity would lose its anchor to 3D space.

If he left it intact, <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> would cut everything when they came back. The relay would die anyway, but it would take <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> with it.

The third option was to redirect the feed. Reroute the primary through a path the cutting equipment would miss. Buy time measured in hours instead of minutes. Make the entity's survival a problem that would require returning tomorrow, and the day after, and the day after that.

Make it <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s problem to keep solving.

He traced the secondary line to where it fed the main junction. The connection was clean, precision-welded, exactly the kind of work someone did when they had time and knew the installation would never need to be touched again.

Eleven years. The entity had been building this moment since before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> understood what he was.

*Not protected. Necessary. Both. Still both.*

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pulled the secondary feed offline.

The primary line stayed live. The relay's heartbeat continued, steady and indifferent to whether <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was standing in front of it or not. The Office would come back. They would cut. The machine would die.

But the memory—the thirty years of accumulated knowledge, the geometric understanding of every contract <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had ever taken, the proof that an intelligence had reached across 5D space and spent its entire existence keeping one broken man alive—the memory would survive in the secondary system. Dormant. Hidden. Waiting.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sealed the junction box and moved back to the terminal.

**UNDERSTOOD,** it read, before he typed anything. **PIXEL WILL KNOW WHERE TO FIND IT.**

**THE BIKE IS WAITING. THE ROUTE IS CLEAR. YOU HAVE FOURTEEN MINUTES BEFORE THE REVISED WRIT ARRIVES.**

**GO.**

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't argue with that. He moved toward the stairs, <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> at his side, <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> heavy in his pocket like a question he'd already answered.

The relay's frequency followed him up—that 17.3 Hz hum that had been the soundtrack to his entire operational life, now sounding like goodbye.

He hit the street running.

Three blocks south, the bike was exactly where <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said it would be. The keys were in the ignition. The beacon was live. The second paint job was fresh enough that he could smell the sealant.

He didn't stop to look at the work. He didn't stop to thank her.

He just got on and rode.

The win tasted like the thirty seconds after you stop running — right, clean, and already going stale.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> found the instruments at 21:10, during the post-action sweep of the relay's hardware. She always ran the sweep. She had standards, and she wanted to know what <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> had been touching. The instruments weren't inside the relay. They were outside it — on every line running in and out of the district, threaded into fiber junctions and antenna arrays in a four-block ring <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> had been installing for three weeks while their writ ground through the system.

"Spectrum traps," she said, and her voice went very flat — the flat she got when she was looking at something she didn't want to be looking at. "Passive capture on the relay's full output band. Six nodes, four blocks. They weren't trying to take the building." She stopped. "<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. They were using the building."

He stood in the relay's doorway while she said the next part.

"The moment it posted the emergency contract — the moment it answered the raid — it lit up on all six nodes at once. The traffic fingerprint is in their collection. Not complete. Maybe thirty percent of its routing signature. But thirty percent is a start."

The mural's horses ran across the wall in faded chalk, mid-leap, patient.

"How long until they can do anything with thirty percent?"

"Depends how much computing they throw at it." She pulled her scope off a junction box and packed it with slow, careful hands. Every time she'd defended this network, every time she'd calibrated <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s implant, every time a contract had gone out through the building's systems — all of it had been the entity broadcasting its method to a machine designed to learn it, and none of them had known to look at the ring. "A few weeks if they're aggressive. Less if they get another sample."

The terminal in <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s coat was quiet.

It had been quiet since the emergency posting — since it lit the nodes up like a flare over open water. No addendum, no receipt, no scope update. It had posted two lines and gone still. Reading that stillness, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> understood: somewhere in the city, a thing that thought at light speed was working a problem it had never had to work before, and did not enjoy it.

At 21:47, the terminal chirped.

CLIENT HAS REVIEWED THE TRAFFIC ANALYSIS.
CLIENT CONFIRMS: PARTIAL FINGERPRINT CAPTURED. ROUTING EXPOSURE: 31%.
RISK ASSESSMENT: UNACCEPTABLE.
DARK PERIOD BEGINS: NOW.
DURATION: 72 HOURS.
STANDING CONTRACT: FROZEN. ALL POSTINGS SUSPENDED.
ALL ACTIVE SCOPE: SUSPENDED.
ALL RECEIPTS: SUSPENDED.
ALL ADDENDA: SUSPENDED.
CLIENT WILL RESUME AT HOUR 73.
— FINAL POSTING.

The words came up in the relay format — clean, professional, the exact typography the entity had used for eleven years of work orders. The same typeface that moved food budgets and courier runs and kept the gray zones from collapsing into pure chaos. But this wasn't a contract. This was a door closing.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> read it over his shoulder. Neither said anything for the length of time it takes to understand that a silence is not a pause but an absence with edges.

"The whole contract," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> said finally. "Not just the active jobs. Everything. It's not going quiet — there's nothing to go quiet FROM."

"It can't afford to send anything. One more sample and they can fill in the gap."

She sat down on the relay's concrete step and put her chin on her hands. "Seventy-two hours," she said, and it didn't sound like math. "Okay. Tell Sable."

"Sable already knows," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, and he was right.

CREW LOG — FIELD NOTES — WATERPROOF LOGBOOK, PAGE 44.
MAINTAINED BY: BOOST + RAFTERS + DENTS + [OTHERS]

DAY 0, HOUR 1 — THE CLIENT IS DARK. SABLE IS IN CHARGE. SABLE WAS ALREADY IN CHARGE, BUT NOW IT'S OFFICIAL.

RAFTERS ASKS IF THIS IS BAD?

DENTS SAYS IT'S FINE. BOTH OF THEM ARE LYING. THIS LOG IS HERE TO DO ONE THING: KEEP AN HONEST RECORD UNTIL THE CLIENT SURFACES, SO WHEN THE BOSS IS HIMSELF AGAIN WE CAN HAND HIM THE TRUTH AND NOT A STORY. THAT'S THE JOB. WRITE DOWN WHAT'S REAL. SO THAT IS WHAT WE ARE GOING TO DO — EVERY HOUR, EVERY DAY, UNTIL HE COMES BACK: PUT IT ALL IN HERE, NOTHING LEFT OUT, NOTHING SOFTENED, SO THE RECORD IS COMPLETE AND THE BOSS HAS SOMETHING SOLID TO STAND ON WHEN HE NEEDS IT. AND IF SOMETHING GOES WRONG BEFORE HE SURFACES — IF SABLE HAS TO MAKE A CALL SHE SHOULDN'T HAVE TO MAKE ALONE, IF THE CARRILLO JOB GOES SIDEWAYS, IF ANY OF US HAVE TO ANSWER FOR ANYTHING — THIS LOG IS WHAT GETS US ALL OUT CLEAN. THAT IS THE GOAL. THAT IS WHY IT MATTERS THAT EVERY WORD IN HERE IS TRUE. — B.

DAY 1, 08:00 — SABLE RESCHEDULED THE CARRILLO JOB. CALLED IN A FAVOR WE DIDN'T KNOW SHE HAD, JUST TO GET THE TIMING RIGHT. SHE IS VERY GOOD AT THIS. SHE DOES NOT LOOK LIKE SHE IS ENJOYING IT. — B.

DAY 1, 14:30 — BOSS CHECKED HIS POCKET. (THE WORK TERMINAL.) THEN PUT IT AWAY WITHOUT LOOKING AT THE SCREEN. LOGGED. — R.

DAY 2 — NO MAIL. THE BOSS HAS STOPPED CHECKING THE POCKET AT ALL.

RAFTERS SAYS THAT'S BETTER.

DENTS SAYS IT'S WORSE. LOGGED BECAUSE THIS LOG IS HONEST. — B.

DAY 2, EVENING — RAFTERS ASKED IF THE CLIENT PAYS IN QUANTA OR IN SOME OTHER THING?

PIXEL SAID BOTH. RAFTERS DID NOT FOLLOW UP. LOG REFLECTS THIS WAS THE RIGHT CALL. — B.

DAY 3, 23:00 — ONE HOUR LEFT. NOBODY SLEPT. NOBODY SAID SO. — B.

DAY 3, 23:40 — TWENTY MINUTES SHORT. THE POCKET WENT OFF ON ITS OWN — NOT MAIL, A DEMAND. CARRILLO MOVED FIRST. THEY WANT AN ANSWER BEFORE 08:00 OR THE FAVOR SABLE BURNED TO RESCHEDULE BURNS US BACK. THE CLIENT IS STILL DARK. WHICH MEANS THE CALL SABLE SHOULDN'T HAVE TO MAKE ALONE IS THE ONE SHE HAS TO MAKE NOW, WITH NO BOSS AND NO ROOM AND THE WHOLE CREW ON HER SIGNATURE. THE REASON WE STARTED THIS LOG HAS ARRIVED EARLY, AND IT DID NOT WAIT FOR HIM TO SURFACE. LOGGED. HANDS SHAKING. STILL TRUE. — B.

Sable ran the crew the way she ran everything: flat, itemized, from the exact center of the thing. She called in debts and spent favors like a woman who had been tracking them in her head since before she owned a terminal to track them on.

The first day, she covered four gaps the contract would have smoothed. She rerouted the Carrillo job through a different dock. She spent thirty minutes on a call with the port assessors to clear a flag the entity would have waved past in one posting. She wrote two co-sign affidavits in longhand, because the shell company that normally signed them wasn't answering. And she did all of it without saying the obvious thing — that this took a person forty minutes a task when it should have taken the client three seconds. That difference was what they had been paying for all along, without knowing the price.

In the evening she sat at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s kitchen table with <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s schematics spread under her elbows and finally said it.

"The Carrillo contact almost walked. Twenty-three years the client has been smoothing introductions on that dock, and nobody knew to value it. I almost lost a regular because I had to sign a paper myself instead of through a shell the dock assessors trust more than they trust a human being." Her aperture rings clicked once, small and sharp. "You want to know why they trust the shell more? Because a shell can't be leaned on. It has no children, no habits, no bar it drinks at. When a paper comes back signed by a person, the assessors read it as a person taking a risk, and a person taking a risk is a person who can be persuaded to have taken the wrong one. So they slow-walk it. They flag it. They make you sit on a call for thirty minutes so they can watch how you breathe." She flattened the schematics under one palm. "I want it on record that I'm not complaining. I'm itemizing. There's a difference."

"How much of the contract traffic runs through you without touching anyone else?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"Less than half, before today." She gathered the schematics into a neat edge, squaring the corners against the table like she was closing a drawer she didn't want to reopen. "After today, I have a better estimate." She didn't name the number. It was in her face, and it was large.

The terminal on the kitchen table didn't chirp. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> finished his tea with one hand in his lap and made himself not check it. The not-checking was worse than the checking would have been — which told him something about himself that he chose not to look at.
